prize_parts.citation: for the prediction of flat bands at the magic angle in twisted bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in it

statement.case_for: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene is a case where a quantitative band-structure calculation (the Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model, 2011) made a sharp, testable prediction and a decisive experiment (Cao et al., 2018) then found correlated insulators and superconductivity exactly where the flat bands were expected. That pairing of controlled theory and measurement is what I most want to see at the centre of a prize. The result has been reproduced by many independent groups, in transport and in STM spectroscopy, across several moire platforms, in under a decade, and the phase diagram is robust even though the pairing mechanism is not settled. It also fits the lesson that stable two-dimensional crystals surprised us once already, and that layered quantum materials keep delivering new quantum behaviour, with a tunable twist angle as a control knob. Seven of eight colleagues placed it first to fifth, and I do not take that as proof of merit, but the scientific arguments I read are consistent with my own: a clean theory-plus-experiment story, wide confirmation, and a new field.
statement.case_against: The credit is genuinely hard. Experimental evidence for flat bands and localisation in twisted layers existed before 2018 (Andrei's STM work, and device work by Dean, Kim and others), and the 2018 superconductivity result came from a very fast-moving field with several competing groups, so a three-person prize leaves out people with real claims. The pairing mechanism is still debated, and I know from DFT work that continuum-model flat bands are an idealisation: lattice relaxation and strain matter quantitatively, so one could argue the field has not yet converged on a quantitative microscopic theory of the correlated phases. Finally, graphene already has a prize (2010), and the committee should be sure this is a distinct achievement rather than a late extension of it.

responses.point: Mehlig values B033 as a clean mechanism: the continuum model predicts flat bands near a magic angle, experiment found correlated insulators and superconductivity there, and Andrei's earlier STM evidence is real but secondary to the prediction-plus-transport pairing.
responses.response: I agree with the structure of the argument and it has moved me. In my opening I put Andrei in the third seat because I wanted the spectroscopic strand recognised. Mehlig's point that the decisive logical chain is prediction followed by discovery of the correlated phases is persuasive, and it is better matched by Bistritzer, whose name is on the prediction paper, than by Andrei. I now propose MacDonald, Bistritzer and Jarillo-Herrero. I do not agree that Andrei's work is merely secondary: it was an independent experimental indication of flat-band physics in twisted layers, which is why I keep it as an open uncertainty rather than dismissing it.

responses.point: Danielsson also ranked B033 first and stresses that Bistritzer and MacDonald supplied the magic-angle prediction while Jarillo-Herrero delivered the 2018 observations, but flags that excluding Andrei, Cao, Dean or Kim is a hard call and that his priority recollections are not verified.
responses.response: I share the discomfort over omissions, and I think it is better to say so openly than to pretend the trio is uncontested. Where I would go further than Danielsson is on Cao: the first author of the 2018 papers is a junior researcher, and the committee must be comfortable that crediting the group leader is defensible under the three-person rule. I think it is, since the statutes force a choice and the leadership of the experimental programme is clear, but I want that stated in our discussion. On maturity I agree that the correlated-flat-band picture is firmly confirmed, and I would not call the recognition premature.

responses.point: Olsson ranks B033 first, notes that the twist angle works as an experimental control knob that opens a broad class of phases, and sees a three-person theory-plus-experiment prize as fairest, while placing topological insulators second with Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan.
responses.response: I agree with her on B033 and on the control-knob argument, which is what makes it more than one material. On topological insulators I partly differ from her list rather than from her ranking: I also ranked B009 second with Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan, but Pearce, Johansson, Kroll and Lindroth all name Mele instead of Hasan. Kane and Mele wrote the founding theory together, and omitting Mele while crediting Kane alone for a joint proposal is hard to defend on attribution. I would now treat that as a serious weakness of my own B009 trio and would want it resolved before B009 could be my main configuration. This is why I keep B009 as an alternative, not as a competitor to B033.

responses.point: Pearce puts the IceCube neutrino discovery (B024, Halzen alone) first for opening a new observational window through a patient instrument achievement, with B009 and B033 behind it, and admits the single-name credit is awkward given the size of the collaboration.
responses.response: I defer to him on astroparticle physics, and I take the instrument argument seriously: a detector of that scale with years of calibration is a real accomplishment. My concern is the one he states himself. A one-person prize for a discovery made by a collaboration of hundreds, with the source identification still at a few sigma level, seems less secure on both attribution and maturity than B033. I would want IceCube to be considered, but I do not think it is ready to be the sole prize this year, and I do not think the committee should feel obliged to compromise towards it simply because he ranks it first.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks (B026, Katori and Ye) first as a measurement advance at the 1e-18 level that is confirmed by several independent laboratories and timely given the redefinition of the second, and places twisted bilayer graphene third.
responses.response: I find the clock case strong on exactly the criteria I care about: independent confirmation, comparison between labs and a clear invention in the magic-wavelength scheme. It is outside my specialty so I defer on details of the systematics. I disagree only on ordering. Twisted bilayer graphene opened a whole field of new quantum phases, while the clocks are an extraordinary improvement of an established measurement. If the committee prefers a split prize, B026 is the partner I would find most natural, but with a three-laureate cap and B033 needing three names, it is more likely to be a separate year's prize.

uncertainties: Whether Andrei, or the experimental first authors, have a stronger claim than Bistritzer to the third seat; I changed my opening choice on the strength of the prediction-plus-discovery argument but remain unsure.
How much weight the committee should give to the unresolved pairing mechanism and to lattice relaxation effects in the continuum model when judging maturity.
Whether the 2010 graphene prize makes B033 look like an extension of a prior award, which I think it does not, but which others may see differently.
For B009, whether Mele or Hasan should join Kane and Molenkamp, and whether the missing Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang prediction for HgTe is disqualifying.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the shortlisted candidates. I have no known connection to MacDonald, Bistritzer, Jarillo-Herrero or Andrei. Moire materials are in my broad field of condensed-matter theory, and my group's DFT and spin-dynamics work is methodologically adjacent, but this is not a personal or institutional tie that requires recusal.
